answers.text: Always the same three lines: delivery date, then item and quantity, then any change from the order. The date line is just the date on its own, and the item line lists the item name together with how many units.
List every claim with date, amount, category and submitter, in that order, and add up all the amounts for the total at the bottom.
The problem here is with the dates, not the price — the €48.50 times 100 is correct. Something about the call date and the delivery date doesn't line up for me.
The 62 versus 54 works out about right, close to 15%. But the on-time figure doesn't — 3 late out of 62 is nearer 95%, not 97%.
I would sign off on the second output, the one showing 25,100 and 612,000. The first one just gives 4.1% without the actual sales and returns figures behind it.

I would send Reply 2, it has the order reference and the credit number in it. Reply 1 doesn't say what actually caused the delay, so that claim can't be checked. That doesn't mean Reply 1 is wrong necessarily, I just wouldn't send it without those same details first.

The pricing and discount figures I would not paste in directly, I'd rather redact them or check the tool is approved first. The confidentiality clause names both companies too, so I'd be careful with that part as well.
Before the report goes out on Friday, I would check the totals against the warehouse system directly rather than only reading over the AI's version.

The extraction step, when it reads the order email, carries the most risk since a mistake there follows through everything after. But the actual checkpoint needs to be at step four, before it sends the confirmation automatically, since that's the point it can't be pulled back.
